extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules governing how foreign patents affect the term of U.S. patents, calculation of patent terms, effects of clerical errors and recording, and statutory requirements/penalties for marking or falsely stamping patented or unpatented articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic patent limited by foreign patent only when inventions identical
rubrics_metrics.description: An American patent is not limited by the term of a foreign patent unless the inventions are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions: Siemens v. Sellers, Ex parte Siemens, Bee Separate Unsworth. If inventions differ in principle, the foreign term does not shorten the domestic patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent limits domestic patent whether open or secret
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign patent limits the duration of a domestic patent regardless of whether the foreign patent is open (published) or secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Gramme Electrical Co. v. Amouz & Hochhausen Electric Co.; courts have treated secret foreign patents as capable of limiting U.S. patent term in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: English 'complete specification' treated as equivalent to issued patent for protection/term purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: An English 'complete specification' gives the same protection as if the patent were already issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson v. Lippert cited; implication is that a complete English specification can operate to limit or affect U.S. patent rights as if the English patent existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: English provisional specification is not a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An English provisional specification does not itself constitute a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson v. Lippert; distinction matters when determining whether a foreign filing or provisional can limit a U.S. patent's term.

rubrics_metrics.name: No English patent complete until final specification is enrolled
rubrics_metrics.description: An English patent is not complete until its final specification is enrolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: McCoburn v. Schroeder, Lorillard v. Dohan. Enrollment timing affects whether the English patent limits a U.S. patent's term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of foreign patent taking effect before domestic grant
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient for the foreign patent to take effect before the actual grant of the domestic patent to trigger limitations — it need not have issued before the U.S. filing in all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later cases relaxed earlier doctrine that a foreign patent must have issued before U.S. filing; courts look to when the foreign patent took effect relative to the domestic grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of foreign patent for term purposes is its issue or publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: When controlling the term of an American patent, the date of the foreign patent is the date of its issue or publication as a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: De Florez v. Raynolds and others; use the foreign patent's official issue/publication date when comparing terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: If domestic and foreign patents granted the same day, domestic may be treated as older
rubrics_metrics.description: When domestic and foreign patents are granted or applications filed on the same day, the domestic patent may be regarded as the older and its term unaffected by the foreign patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Mann and related cases: simultaneous grants/applications can prevent foreign limitation of the U.S. term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where U.S. application antedates foreign application, foreign may not limit U.S. term
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application in the United States antedates an application in England (or a foreign filing), and the American patent issues before the foreign patent is sealed/enrolled, the foreign filing has no effect on the American patent's term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson v. Lippert; priority of filing/issue can preserve U.S. term against later foreign grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of domestic patent fixed by remaining term of foreign patent as originally granted
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix the term of an American patent limited by a prior foreign patent, ascertain how long the foreign patent, as originally granted, was to run after the issue of the domestic patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paillard v. Bruno, Ex parte Siemens. Calculate remainder of foreign patent's original term measured from the domestic patent's issue date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent's original granted term controls even if later extended or forfeited
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a foreign patent, insofar as it affects a domestic patent, is the term originally granted, regardless of later statutory extensions or forfeitures for nonpayment of fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Gillett and others: subsequent extension or forfeiture of the foreign patent does not retroactively alter the U.S. patent's term set by the foreign patent's original grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacatur of foreign patent does not limit domestic patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If a foreign patent that was limiting the term of a domestic patent is vacated ab initio, the domestic patent is not limited thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bate Refrigerating Co. v. Gillett: annulment of foreign patent does not necessarily shrink U.S. rights that were calculated against it at issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for extension of foreign patent not part of the original grant
rubrics_metrics.description: The capability of extension under foreign law is not part of the original grant that measures the domestic patent's term; extensions do not prolong the U.S. monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions under foreign law are considered separate and do not retroactively lengthen U.S. patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: New grants/additions (improvements) treated as separate patents with own terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an original patent is enlarged by new grants for improvements, each new grant is treated as a different patent with its own issue date and term; it does not remove the original patent's limitation on the American patent's term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements result in distinct patents rather than extensions of the original patent's term for U.S. purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premature expiration of foreign patent (noncompliance) does not extinguish domestic patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The premature expiration of the foreign patent for failure to comply with conditions does not extinguish the American patent nor curtail the term fixed by the foreign patent at the time it was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeiture of foreign rights after issuance does not retroactively shorten the U.S. patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of domestic patent term when not limited by foreign patents (term measured from issue date)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent's duration is not affected by a prior foreign patent, the day of its date is excluded and the patent will expire on the last hour of the same day and month seventeen years after its issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson v. McCullough cited; standard U.S. rule for term computation (17 years from issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate patents for different inventions expire separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate patents for different inventions, having separate dates, each expire at the end of their own term even if neither invention is capable of use without the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McKay v. Dibert: independence of patent terms despite interdependence of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents have distinct, elected shorter terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents have different limitation options and are granted for three and a half, seven, or fourteen years as the inventor elects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents are governed by their own statutory term choices and not by the 17-year utility term rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere clerical errors in patent do not affect validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere clerical mistakes (e.g., a mistake in the Christian name or a single-letter error in the surname) do not affect the patent's validity if the patentee is otherwise sufficiently described; such errors are corrected on the record at patentee's request if due to Patent Office fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material errors must be remedied by reissue or disclaimer; immaterial defects receive liberal construction in favor of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant/title not complete until patent is recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of a patent is not complete, nor does any title pass, until the patent is recorded in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Osgood and Boyden v. Burke: recording is required to perfect the title of record; after recording the title is enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of patent is constructive notice and records open to inspection; certified copies have evidentiary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: All letters-patent are recorded with their specifications; the record is constructive notice of its contents and binding; records, specifications, drawings, models, and related documents are open to inspection and certified copies (for lawful fees) are evidence with the same weight as originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brooks v. Jenkins and other cited authorities; practical note that certified transcripts may be corrected by new transcript if incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordings not required by law give no notice; partial recording can bind those acting on recorded parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of an instrument which the law does not require to be recorded is no notice; where some papers are recorded and others not, a person acting upon the recorded ones in ignorance of the others is bound as if the unrecorded papers were present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton v. Kingsbury and related cases illustrate the interplay between recorded and unrecorded documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented articles must be marked to give public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone making or vending patented articles for or under the patentee must give sufficient notice to the public that the article is patented, by marking the article with the word 'patented' together with the date of the patent, or, where impracticable, affixing a label to the article or its package containing the same information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply bars recovery of more than nominal damages unless the patentee proves actual notice in some equivalent manner; marking may be on package if marking the article itself is impracticable (Sessions v. Romadka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of marking and manufacturer responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to mark patented articles and the date of marking devolves upon the manufacturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York Pharmaceutical Association v. Tilden: patentees must give 'sufficient notice ... together with the day and year the patent was granted' by stamping or labelling; verbal/written equivalent notice that includes the date is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substantial damages for unstamped articles unless notice or knowledge; extent of liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Sec. 4900 (statute), no recovery of substantial damages can be had while articles are unstamped unless notice is given or the infringer had knowledge; even then liability for substantial damages generally only attaches for infringements committed with knowledge or after notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allen v. Deacon and Allen-related cases: burden on patentee to show notice or the infringer's knowledge to recover beyond nominal damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on stamping by infringers or unauthorized persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the patentee, assigns, legal representatives, or those authorized to practice under the patent may mark an article with the patentee's name or with words such as 'patented', 'patentee', or 'letters-patent'; others are prohibited from marking or imitating such marks with intent to counterfeit or deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Haish and related authority: prohibition protects patentees from fraudulent imitation and the public from confusion; wrongful marking carries penalties distinct from infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamper's right does not include marking to show made under another's patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A person does not have the right to mark goods with any indicia showing they are made under another's patent which he does not own; marking under another's patent without authority is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton v. Kingsbury commentary: owner/ licensee regulates quality of goods bearing patent-mark; unauthorized use can harm the patent's value and mislead the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on marking unpatented articles as 'patent' aimed at preventing fraud; intent required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an offense to mark or affix the word 'patent' (or similar) to any unpatented article for the purpose of deceiving the public; the offense requires an intent to deceive — marking in jest or in the honest belief of patentability does not constitute the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walker v. Hawkwurst, Nichols v. Newell, and others: courts examine intent; the word 'patent' is prima facie an assertion that the article has merit and was patented, creating a presumption of deceptive intent unless rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive is a question of fact for the jury (except in extreme cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there was an 'intent to deceive' by falsely marking is ordinarily a question for the jury, though in extreme cases the court might rule as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walker v. Hawkwurst and Nichols v. Newell: factual inquiries about whether the public could be misled; evidence of belief that a patent is expected may not defeat liability if intent to deceive exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking an article 'patented' when a patent is expected may be lawful absent intent to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may be marked 'patented' when a patent is expected if there is no intent to deceive (e.g., manufacturer expects patent to issue shortly); unlawful only if done with fraudulent intent to deceive the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nichols v. Newell: marking in anticipation of a patent can still constitute offense if intended to deceive for a period of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking that cannot possibly deceive (e.g., evidently not patentable) is not an offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Marking with 'patented' on an article that is evidently not patentable and which cannot deceive the public is not an offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. v. Morris: context matters; if no one could reasonably be misled, criminal penalty may not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory penalty and qui tam enforcement for false stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute imposing penalties for false stamping is penal and must be strictly construed; punishment is a fine (historically $100) and costs, recoverable by a qui tam action in the U.S. District Court within whose jurisdiction the offense occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure notes: action is typically brought in the name of the informer (not the United States) and various cases (Tompkins v. Butterfield, Winne v. Snow) discuss enforcement and standing.
